key_insight: Patient-level splits prevent subject leakage but cannot rule out acquisition-related confounding that may drive apparent diagnostic performance.
clinical_relevance: High breast thermography benchmark performance may reflect when patients were scanned rather than pathology, limiting its value as evidence for clinical use.
method: Audit five questions covering confounder predictiveness, image decodability, score dependence, added image value and discrimination after control.
Evaluate acquisition-date confounding across nine imaging arms using patient-disjoint splits.
Repeat the audit in an independently acquired cohort with age as the dominant confounding channel.
evidence_signal: In 236 DMR-IR patients, acquisition date alone achieved AUROC 0.980 versus 0.949 for the best imaging arm; no arm improved on date in paired-fold comparisons.
watch_item: Only eight cross-label same-date pairs from ten patients limit evaluation within acquisition-date groups, so confounder mitigation alone cannot establish that remaining discrimination reflects pathology.
paper_title: Leakage-Free Is Not Confounder-Free: What a Patient-Level Split Cannot Certify About a Medical Imaging Benchmark
